extracted.intended_audience: advertising and PR professionals; marketers; industry observers
extracted.subtask_description: Lessons and immediate actions for brands and agencies when an ad sparks public backlash, focusing on apology, content removal, team composition, and social monitoring. Also guidance for ad production choices (in-house vs. external).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity on creative team
rubrics_metrics.description: “served as a cautionary tale for not having enough diversity on your creative team”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lack of diversity can produce tone-deaf creative that misreads cultural and political contexts; the piece cites the ad as emblematic of problems from a monocultural workplace (see related commentary titled 'When black and brown is not enough').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating ads entirely in-house / seek external objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: “or attempting to create your ads entirely in-house.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-house production can lack objectivity and lead to misjudged work — industry commenters noted 'Ad was done in-house. No objectivity.' Brands should consider outside agencies or independent review to catch blind spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not co-opt or trivialize protest movements / be sensitive to serious issues
rubrics_metrics.description: The ad “struck critics as a lazy attempt to co-opt recent protest movements such as Black Lives Matter and the Women’s March on Washington.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using imagery or narratives that appear to appropriate or minimize real social movements; creators should ensure they are not 'making light of any serious issue' and test concepts with representative audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt apology and removal / halt further rollout when you 'miss the mark'
rubrics_metrics.description: Company statement: “Clearly we missed the mark, and we apologize... We are removing the content and halting any further rollout.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When backlash is swift and severe, swift acknowledgement, apology, and removing/pausing distribution can be necessary; statements should show accountability (e.g., apologizing for putting talent in a difficult position).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor social media and be prepared to correct messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sign the brand backed away was when Brad Jakeman deleted a Tweet; by 1:30 the brand released a statement and pulled the ad off YouTube as backlash mounted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active social monitoring is essential; brands should be ready to delete or correct problematic posts, escalate to leadership, and issue coordinated responses as required by the volume and tone of reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using celebrities in politically sensitive narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Company apology: “We also apologize for putting Kendall Jenner in this position.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using high-profile talent in politically or culturally sensitive creative can intensify criticism and harm the individual's reputation; evaluate risks to both brand and talent before approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removing official content may not stop circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: “The spot continues to live online, however, thanks to the many other people who posted it over the past 24 hours.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brands must recognize that deleting an official post does not erase copies; crisis planning should include strategies for managing reposts, search results, and ongoing conversation rather than assuming removal ends the issue.
